title: The split-probe swap test
takeaway: A representation of an unspoken intermediate, extracted without the J-lens, keeps most of its variance outside the J-space — yet swapping only its small J-space component flips the model's answer on 61% of 90 two-hop prompts, matching the raw J-lens swap at 60%, while swapping the much larger remainder succeeds on only 28%, and on 6% once the J-space coordinates are held fixed.
walkthrough:
The preceding swap experiments showed that exchanging [[jacobian-lens]] vectors redirects the model's [[internal-reasoning]]. This figure, rendered in the article as a live widget rather than a static image, tests something stronger: whether the [[j-space]] is privileged among everything the model knows about an intermediate, or merely one place among many where the same information could be intervened on.

The left panel walks one example. The prompt is a two-hop question whose unspoken bridging concept is China. An [[intermediate-probe]] for that concept is built without the lens: the mean [[residual-stream]] activation over prompts that imply China through different surface cues, minus the mean over all intermediates. [[gradient-pursuit]] then splits the probe against the J-lens dictionary into two parts. One part is the [[j-space-component]]: a nonnegative combination of $k=25$ J-lens vectors, whose top entries the panel prints. The other part is the leftover remainder, orthogonal to that combination. The split is lopsided. The J-space part typically explains only about 10–15% of the probe's variance; the remainder carries the rest.

Columns beside the split show the model's next-token distribution under four conditions: no intervention, a raw China↔France [[lens-coordinate-swap]] of the kind used earlier in the section, a swap along only the probe's J-space component, and a swap along only the remainder.

The right panel aggregates over $n=90$ two-hop prompts. Each bar is the fraction of trials on which that swap places the target-appropriate answer at the top of the output distribution, with [[wilson-interval]] error bars. Swapping the J-space component succeeds on 61% of trials, matching the 60% of the raw J-lens swap. Swapping the remainder, despite its far larger share of the variance, succeeds on only 28%.

The hatched bars repeat each component swap while the complementary component is clamped to its value from the clean forward pass. Under that control, the remainder swap's success rate falls from 28% to 6%. So even the remainder's residual effect appears to act by perturbing the J-space coordinates downstream, rather than through a separate channel.

The paper's reading is correspondingly two-sided: most of the model's working representation of an inferred intermediate lies outside the J-space, but the part that mediates the reasoning is the J-space component.

terms.definition: A J-lens-free representation of the unspoken intermediate: the mean residual-stream activation over prompts that imply the same intermediate through different surface cues, minus the mean over all intermediates.
The part of the probe reconstructable as a nonnegative combination of k=25 J-lens vectors, found by gradient pursuit; it typically explains only about 10–15% of the probe's variance.
The leftover part of the probe after the J-space component is removed; it carries the bulk of the probe's variance.
The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm used to find the nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors that best reconstructs the probe.
The J-lens vectors with the largest coefficients in the probe's J-space component, printed in the left panel to show what the component names in vocabulary terms.
The unspoken bridging concept of the worked example's two-hop prompt: the intermediate the model must infer but never says.
The alternative concept swapped in for China; a successful swap makes the model answer as if the intermediate had been France.
A factual question answerable only by first inferring a bridging entity that appears in neither the prompt nor the answer, then reasoning from it.
The control column: the model's next-token distribution on an unmodified forward pass.
The baseline intervention from the section's earlier experiments: exchanging the activation's coordinates along the two concepts' single J-lens token vectors at every position.
The model's output probabilities over the vocabulary at the answer position, shown per column so the effect of each swap on the answer is directly visible.
The success criterion for the right panel's bars: the proportion of the 90 prompts on which the swap moves the target-appropriate answer to the most likely output token.
The error bars on the success-rate bars: Wilson-score confidence intervals for a proportion.

The clamped control condition: the same component swap, but with the complementary component held (clamped) at its clean-pass value throughout the forward pass, so the swap cannot act by indirectly perturbing the other component.
One direction per vocabulary token per layer, from the Jacobian lens; the dictionary against which the probe is decomposed.

numbers.meaning: The number of two-hop prompts in the systematic comparison; each contributes one trial per swap condition.
The sparsity of the gradient-pursuit decomposition: the probe's J-space component is a nonnegative combination of 25 J-lens vectors.
The share of the probe's variance the J-space component typically explains; the paper cites this to stress how small the causally dominant part is relative to the remainder.

Success rate of swapping only the probe's J-space component: on 61% of the 90 prompts the target answer reaches top-1. This matches the raw lens swap, so the small component carries essentially the full effect.
Success rate of the raw J-lens token-vector swap on the same 90 prompts, the baseline the component swaps are compared against.
Success rate of swapping only the non-J-space remainder. Despite holding most of the probe's variance, it flips the answer on barely more than a quarter of trials.

Success rate of the remainder swap when the intermediate's J-space coordinates are clamped to their clean-pass values: the remainder's residual effect mostly vanishes, indicating it was itself routed through the J-space.
The confidence level of the Wilson intervals on the success-rate bars.
The success threshold: a swap counts only if the target-appropriate answer becomes the model's single most likely next token.
